title: Three visitors at Mamre (Genesis 18:1–15)
hookLine: Abraham runs to feed three strangers; Christians painted them as the Trinity

cards: A Russian icon, painted by a monk, is copied onto cards and walls far from Russia. Three winged figures sit around a table, heads tilted toward one another, a cup in the middle.
The fourth side of the table, the side facing you, is empty, as if a place were left open. The painter, Andrei Rublev, didn't invent the scene.
The icon is known as the Trinity, but what it shows is a moment from Genesis: an old man's lunch with three strangers who showed up at noon.

teach.h: THE DOOR OF THE TENT, AT NOON.
teach.b: First, the scene. Abraham is sitting at the door of his tent by the oaks of Mamre, in the Douay-Rheims, "in the very heat of the day." The worst hour to have guests.
He looks up and sees three men standing nearby, and the old man doesn't wait: "he ran to meet them from the door of his tent" and bowed to the ground.
Second, the feast. He offers a little water and a morsel of bread, and then makes it much more. He hurries to Sarah: three measures of fine flour, make cakes.
He runs to the herd for a tender calf. He brings butter and milk, and stands by them under the tree while they eat. A morsel turns into a banquet.
Third, who they are. The text keeps shifting. Three men.
Then the Lord speaks. Then two of them go on toward Sodom as angels. Genesis never explains it.

teach.h: THREE MEN, THE LORD, OR ANGELS?
teach.b: Jewish tradition reads the three as angels sent by God. Some Christian writers, Ambrose and Augustine among them, saw a hint of the Trinity, which is what Rublev painted.
And one visitor makes a promise: by this time next year, Sarah will have a son. Behind the tent door, Sarah laughs. Fourth, what the Church took from it.
The Letter to the Hebrews says not to forget hospitality, because some, by it, have entertained angels without knowing.
Saint Benedict told his monks to welcome every guest as Christ himself.
In Greek, hospitality is philoxenia: love of the stranger.

how: Benedictine monasteries still follow Saint Benedict's rule to receive every guest as Christ, and Rublev's icon of the three visitors, often called the Trinity, is used for prayer by Catholics and Orthodox Christians alike.

o: love of the stranger, welcoming guests well
politeness owed only to family and friends
a fee paid to stay at an inn overnight

s: Abraham waits for the strangers to ask for help
he runs to meet them in the heat of the day and bows to the ground.
Genesis explains exactly who the three visitors are
the text shifts between three men, the Lord, and angels. Jewish and Christian readers interpret it differently.
Saint Benedict told his monks to welcome guests as Christ
and Hebrews says some have entertained angels without knowing.

games.q: you're Abraham, old now, resting at your tent door in the worst heat of the day. three strangers appear nearby. what do you do?
o: run to meet them, and turn a morsel of bread into a feast.
send a servant to ask their business.
games.why: he runs, bows, and has Sarah bake cakes while he fetches a tender calf. the visitors carry a promise: a son by next year.

practice: Picture the next person likely to come through your door or join your table: a friend, a delivery driver, a coworker, a child's friend after school.
Then picture Abraham running in the heat, and choose what you could offer that's a little more than a morsel: a real drink, a chair, your full attention, something from the good shelf.
If you pray, ask to see Christ in whoever comes.

wordCard.voice: Hospitality. Philoxenia in Greek, love of the stranger. Abraham running at noon to feed three visitors who turn out to carry God's promise.

orig.note: Greek: hospitality, literally love of the stranger. the word in Hebrews 13:2.
